turns.prompt_text: I got these three antenna off of a modem Can I connect them to an esp32? Attached 1 file. - 1a2fdccb-333e-4209-96e9-2b9a4572874e
turns.response_html:
Yes, you can theoretically connect them to an ESP32, but there are a few important hardware, frequency, and connection hurdles you need to clear first.

Looking at the photo, these look like standard "rubber ducky" dipole antennas that have either been cut, pulled out of their standard threaded connectors (SMA/RP-SMA), or desoldered directly from a modem's internal PCB.

Here is what you need to consider to make this work:

1. The Frequency Match

An ESP32 operates strictly on the 2.4 GHz band for Wi-Fi and Bluetooth.

  • If the modem was a Wi-Fi router: These antennas are tuned for 2.4 GHz (and likely 5 GHz), meaning they will work great and offer solid impedance matching ($50\ \Omega$).
  • If the modem was a cellular gateway (LTE/5G): They are tuned for different bands (like 700 MHz, 1.9 GHz, etc.). They will technically still transmit and receive signals if connected, but your range will be poor due to a high Standing Wave Ratio (SWR), which wastes RF energy as heat.

2. Your ESP32 Module Type

You cannot easily add an external antenna to a standard ESP32 that relies on an onboard PCB trace antenna (the zig-zag gold line on the board).

  • If you have a U.FL / IPEX version (e.g., ESP32-WROOM-32U): These boards come with a tiny, round gold receptacle specifically designed for an external antenna. This is the ideal candidate.
  • If you have a standard PCB antenna version: You would have to manually desolder a microscopic zero-ohm jumper resistor near the antenna feed to disconnect the built-in trace, then carefully solder your external antenna wire to the tiny RF pads. It requires steady hands and a fine-tip soldering iron.

3. Dealing with the Damaged Wires

Because these antennas lack standard screw-on connectors right now, you have two routing options:

Option A: Direct Soldering (Most Likely)

Looking at the antenna on the left, you have an exposed length of coaxial cable. Coaxial cable has two parts: an inner core wire (signal) and an outer braided metal shield (ground).

  1. Strip the outer jacket carefully.
  2. Separate the outer shield braid and twist it into a lead.
  3. Strip the insulation off the tiny inner core.
  4. Solder the inner core directly to the ESP32's antenna signal pad, and the outer shield to the adjacent RF ground pad. Keep these exposed leads as incredibly short as possible (under 2–3mm) to prevent signal loss or interference.

Option B: Splicing a Pigtail

You can buy a cheap U.FL to RP-SMA pigtail cable, cut it in half, and carefully solder/splice the tiny internal coax wires to the exposed pins on the bottom of the middle or right antennas. This allows you to easily plug it into an ESP32-U module.

Since they are tuned for 4G (LTE), using them with an ESP32 is going to be a bit of a mismatch.

4G LTE networks utilize a wide variety of frequency bands. Depending on the carrier and the modem, these antennas are likely optimized for bands around 700 MHz, 850 MHz, 1.7 GHz (AWS), or 1.9 GHz.

The ESP32, however, operates strictly on the 2.4 GHz spectrum for Wi-Fi and Bluetooth.

Here is what happens if you try to cross them over, along with a better alternative for your project:

The Problem: Impedance and SWR

Antennas are cut to precise physical lengths corresponding to the wavelength of the frequency they are meant to broadcast.

Because a 4G antenna is physically tuned for longer wavelengths (lower frequencies) than 2.4 GHz, connecting it to an ESP32 causes a severe mismatch in impedance. This leads to a high SWR (Standing Wave Ratio).

Instead of cleanly radiating the 2.4 GHz signal into the air, a significant portion of the RF energy will reflect back down the wire into the ESP32's transmitter.

  • The Result: You will get incredibly poor Wi-Fi range—potentially worse than the tiny built-in PCB trace antenna.
  • The Risk: In extreme scenarios with high-power transmitters, high reflected energy can overheat and fry the RF front-end. Because the ESP32 is a low-power ($+20\text{ dBm}$ max) device, you likely won't destroy it, but the performance will be disappointing.

A Better Fix for an ESP32

If you want to maximize your ESP32's range, you are much better off using an antenna natively tuned for 2.4 GHz.

If your ESP32 module has a U.FL (IPEX) connector, look for a dedicated 2.4 GHz rubber ducky antenna with a U.FL-to-RP-SMA pigtail adapter. Alternatively, you can use a small, flexible 2.4 GHz PCB/FPC adhesive antenna that plugs directly into the board. These are inexpensive and will vastly outperform a mismatched 4G antenna.

Are you working with a standard ESP32 development board that has the integrated gold zig-zag antenna on the PCB, or does your board have the tiny round external antenna connector?

How to Proceed

Since the frequency hurdle is cleared, you just have to tackle the physical connection we talked about earlier:

  • Identify the wires: The stripped wire on the left antenna contains a central signal wire and an outer ground shield braid.
  • If your ESP32 has a U.FL connector: It's usually easiest to buy a cheap U.FL pigtail cable, cut it, and splice the microscopic coax wires together.

What specific model or variant of the ESP32 board are you planning to attach these to?

Looking at the image, you have a standard ESP32 development board (it uses a module similar to the ESP32-WROOM-32D).

The short answer is: Technically yes, but practically no. I highly recommend against modifying this specific board.

Here is a breakdown of why this is the toughest board to work with for your salvaged antennas, and what your options are.

The Hardware Hurdle

If you look closely at the very top of the board (above the metal shield with your pink sticky note), you can see a zig-zag pattern in the black PCB. That is the integrated trace antenna.

Crucially, this board does not have a U.FL/IPEX connector.

Because of this, the RF signal path is hardwired directly from the chip under the metal shield straight into that copper zig-zag trace. There are no easy solder pads or zero-ohm resistors on this specific layout to easily reroute the signal.

The "Scavenger Engineer" Route (Not Recommended)

To physically connect your salvaged 2.4 GHz antennas to this board, you would have to perform some extreme micro-surgery:

  1. Sever the trace: You would need to take an X-Acto knife and physically cut the copper trace leading to the zig-zag antenna to disconnect it.
  2. Scrape the board: You'd have to scrape away the black solder mask near the cut to expose the bare RF copper trace, as well as a nearby ground plane.
  3. Micro-solder: You would then solder the microscopic inner core of your stripped coaxial cable to the tiny exposed RF trace, and the outer braided shield to the ground plane.

The catch: Even if your hands are incredibly steady, doing this by hand almost guarantees a massive impedance mismatch. The trace was not designed to have a coaxial cable tapped into it. Instead of improving your range, this hack job usually results in terrible signal loss, noise, and worse performance than the onboard antenna.

Given that you have been experimenting with RF sensing and Wi-Fi-based positional tracking, having reliable, predictable signal integrity is crucial. A hacked trace will likely throw off your positional data completely.

The Better Solution

Keep this board exactly as it is and use it for projects where standard Wi-Fi range is sufficient.

For your salvaged router antennas, you should pick up an ESP32-WROOM-32U development board. The "U" designates that it lacks the zig-zag trace antenna and instead has a tiny, gold U.FL connector pre-installed on the module. You can buy a cheap U.FL to RP-SMA pigtail cable, cut it, splice it directly to your salvaged antenna wires, and snap it right onto the board for a perfect, impedance-matched connection.

turns.response_html:
You definitely can straight solder it if you want to experiment, but it comes with a few technical realities—and the Raspberry Pi Pico is a fascinating alternative to look at here.

Let's break down the soldering reality first, and then look at how the Pico handles radio waves.

1. Straight Soldering: Is it a good idea?

If you buy an ESP32 board with a U.FL connector (the tiny gold circle receptor), trying to solder a thick coax cable directly onto that microscopic pad is incredibly difficult. The heat from a soldering iron can easily delaminate the pad right off the board.

If you want to use these specific salvaged antennas without buying extra connectors, your best bet is a hybrid approach:

  1. Buy a cheap pack of U.FL pigtail cables (they usually cost a couple of dollars for a multi-pack).
  2. Snipping the big screw-on end off the pigtail leaves you with a tiny U.FL connector on one side and bare coaxial wire on the other.
  3. You can then easily solder the bare wire of the pigtail to the bare wire of your salvaged antenna.
  4. Finally, you just snap the U.FL side cleanly onto the board.

This protects the ESP32 board from intense soldering iron heat and maintains a much cleaner, impedance-matched signal path.

2. Raspberry Pi Pico vs. Antennas

To clear up a common hardware misconception: Microcontrollers don't actually "run" antennas; the onboard radio chip does. An antenna is just a piece of shaped metal that allows electromagnetic waves to transfer efficiently into a circuit. The amount of computational horsepower (CPU speed or RAM) a microcontroller has doesn't dictate whether an antenna works.

Instead, it depends entirely on which version of the Pico you have:

Standard Raspberry Pi Pico

The base Raspberry Pi Pico has no wireless chip at all. It has plenty of compute capacity for general electronics, but connecting an antenna to it directly won't do anything because there is no radio hardware to generate or receive a high-frequency signal.

Raspberry Pi Pico W (Wireless Version)

The Pico W features an onboard Infineon CYW43439 wireless chip, giving it 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi and Bluetooth capabilities.

However, the Pico W faces the exact same physical challenge as your current ESP32:

  • It uses a built-in, proprietary onboard PCB antenna (designed by ABRACON).
  • There is no external antenna jack.
  • To attach your salvaged antennas, you would have to scratch, cut, and micro-solder directly onto the Pico's delicate circuit board, which ruins the tuning of the radio.

What's the best path forward?

If your goal is to build a high-range project (like the remote monitoring setup for your friend's bee traps), your cleanest and most reliable option is to grab an ESP32-WROOM-32U development board.

Because it lacks an onboard trace and features a dedicated external port, it will pair perfectly with a cheap U.FL pigtail spliced onto your salvaged Cradlepoint antennas. This setup gives you maximum range and steady signal data without risking a messy soldering job on a standard board.

Are you looking to get maximum possible distance out of this setup, or are you mostly trying to see how much range you can squeeze out of salvaged parts?

turns.prompt_text: So you can see here here that the end of this antenna is some kind of coaxial cable sheathing translucent material I don't know how I would connect this Attached 1 file. - a942ad53-92e8-40e5-927e-fb8151ada0c9
turns.response_html:
That close-up picture makes the anatomy of your salvaged antenna wire perfectly clear. You are dealing with standard miniature coaxial cable.

To connect this to anything cleanly, you have to separate its two nested electrical pathways: the outer ground shield and the inner signal core.

Here is exactly what you are looking at in your photo, and how to prep it for a connection.

The Anatomy of Your Wire

  • The Outer Braided Mesh: This is your Ground (GND). It protects the signal from external electromagnetic interference.
  • The Translucent Layer: This is the Dielectric Insulator. Its only job is to physically separate the outer shield from the inner wire so they don't short out.
  • The Hidden Center Core: Dead center inside that translucent material sits a very thin copper or silver wire. This is your Signal pin (RF).

Step-by-Step: How to Prep and Connect It

If you want to straight-solder this or splice it to a pigtail adapter, you have to carefully unwrap it like a nested doll.

Step 1: Separate the Ground Shield

Using a safety pin, tweezers, or a small pick, gently poke at the bottom of the silver braided mesh to loosen the weave. Carefully unbraid the tiny wires and bunch them off to one side. Twist them together tightly into a single wire lead.

Step 2: Expose the Core Signal Wire

Now you will see just the translucent tube sticking out. Use an X-Acto knife or very precise wire strippers to gently score the translucent plastic about 2–3 millimeters from the end. Carefully pull the plastic cap off to reveal the bare center copper wire. Be incredibly gentle—if you nick the center conductor, it will snap off easily.

Step 3: Making the Connection

Once separated, you have two distinct leads:

  1. The Twisted Shield (Ground) 2. The Exposed Center Core (Signal)
  • If splicing to a U.FL pigtail cable: You would prep the cut end of the pigtail the exact same way. Solder the pigtail's center core to the antenna's center core, and slide a tiny piece of heat-shrink tubing over it. Then, twist and solder the two outer ground shields together, and seal the whole joint with a larger piece of heat shrink to keep it rigid.
  • If soldering directly to a board (like an external antenna module): The center core gets soldered directly to the tiny pad labeled ANT or RF, and the twisted braid gets soldered to the adjacent pad labeled GND. Keep these exposed leads under 3mm long, as any unshielded length acts like an un-tuned antenna and introduces noise.

Do you have an adjustable-temperature soldering iron and some thin heat-shrink tubing on hand for this?
